y1.text: Siddhartha spared him and let him do as he pleased, he honoured his mourning. Siddhartha understood that his son did not know him, that he could not love him like a father. Slowly, he also saw and understood that the eleven-year-old was a pampered boy, a mother's boy, and that he had grown up in the habits of rich people, accustomed to finer food, to a soft bed, accustomed to giving orders to servants. Siddhartha understood that the mourning, pampered child could not suddenly and willingly be content with a life among strangers and in poverty. He did not force him, he did many a chore for him, always picked the best piece of the meal for him. Slowly, he hoped to win him over, by friendly patience.

y2.text: "Pardon me," he said, "from a friendly heart, I'm talking to you. I'm seeing that you are tormenting yourself, I'm seeing that you're in grief. Your son, my dear, is worrying you, and he is also worrying me. That young bird is accustomed to a different life, to a different nest. He has not, like you, ran away from riches and the city, being disgusted and fed up with it; against his will, he had to leave all this behind. I asked the river, O friend, many times I have asked it. But the river laughs, it laughs at me, it laughs at you and me, and is shaking with laughter at our foolishness. Water wants to join water, youth wants to join youth, your son is not in the place where he can prosper. You too should ask the river; you too should listen to it!"

y3.text: "I knew it. You don't force him, don't beat him, don't give him orders, because you know that 'soft' is stronger than 'hard,' water stronger than rocks, love stronger than force. Very good, I praise you. But aren't you mistaken in thinking that you wouldn't force him, wouldn't punish him? Don't you shackle him with your love? Don't you make him feel inferior every day, and don't you make it even harder on him with your kindness and patience? Don't you force him, the arrogant and pampered boy, to live in a hut with two old banana-eaters, to whom even rice is a delicacy, whose thoughts can't be his, whose hearts are old and quiet and beat in a different pace than his? Isn't he forced, isn't he punished by all this?"

y4.text: Would you think, my dear, anybody might perhaps be spared from taking this path? That perhaps your little son would be spared, because you love him, because you would like to keep him from suffering and pain and disappointment? But even if you would die ten times for him, you would not be able to take the slightest part of his destiny upon yourself."

y5.text: Never before had Vasudeva spoken so many words. Kindly, Siddhartha thanked him, went troubled into the hut, could not sleep for a long time. Vasudeva had told him nothing, he had not already thought and known for himself. But this was a knowledge he could not act upon, stronger than the knowledge was his love for the boy, stronger was his tenderness, his fear to lose him. Had he ever lost his heart so much to something, had he ever loved any person thus, thus blindly, thus sufferingly, thus unsuccessfully, and yet thus happily?

y6.text: But now, since his son was here, now he, Siddhartha, had also become completely a childlike person, suffering for the sake of another person, loving another person, lost to a love, having become a fool on account of love. Now he too felt, late, once in his lifetime, this strongest and strangest of all passions, suffered from it, suffered miserably, and was nevertheless in bliss, was nevertheless renewed in one respect, enriched by one thing.

y7.text: Through all this, the son let him commit his foolish acts, let him court for his affection, let him humiliate himself every day by giving in to his moods. This father had nothing which would have delighted him and nothing which he would have feared. He was a good man, this father, a good, kind, soft man, perhaps a very devout man, perhaps a saint, all these were no attributes which could win the boy over. He was bored by this father, who kept him prisoner here in this miserable hut of his, he was bored by him, and for him to answer every naughtiness with a smile, every insult with friendliness, every viciousness with kindness, this very thing was the hated trick of this old sneak. Much more the boy would have liked it if he had been threatened by him, if he had been abused by him.

y8.text: "We will build a raft," said Vasudeva, "to get our boat back, which the boy has taken away. But him, you shall let run along, my friend, he is no child any more, he knows how to get around. He's looking for the path to the city, and he is right, don't forget that. He's doing what you've failed to do yourself. He's taking care of himself, he's taking his course. Alas, Siddhartha, I see you suffering, but you're suffering a pain at which one would like to laugh, at which you'll soon laugh for yourself."

y9.text: When Siddhartha had already been walking through the forest for a long time, the thought occurred to him that his search was useless. Either, so he thought, the boy was far ahead and had already reached the city, or, if he should still be on his way, he would conceal himself from him, the pursuer. As he continued thinking, he also found that he, on his part, was not worried for his son, that he knew deep inside that he had neither perished nor was in any danger in the forest. Nevertheless, he ran without stopping, no longer to save him, just to satisfy his desire, just to perhaps see him one more time. And he ran up to just outside of the city.

y10.text: After having been standing by the gate of the garden for a long time, Siddhartha realised that his desire was foolish, which had made him go up to this place, that he could not help his son, that he was not allowed to cling him. Deeply, he felt the love for the runaway in his heart, like a wound, and he felt at the same time that this wound had not been given to him in order to turn the knife in it, that it had to become a blossom and had to shine.

y11.text: Instantly, he recognised this touch, this tender, bashful touch, and regained his senses. He rose and greeted Vasudeva, who had followed him. And when he looked into Vasudeva's friendly face, into the small wrinkles, which were as if they were filled with nothing but his smile, into the happy eyes, then he smiled too. Now he saw the bananas lying in front of him, picked them up, gave one to the ferryman, ate the other one himself. After this, he silently went back into the forest with Vasudeva, returned home to the ferry. Neither one talked about what had happened today, neither one mentioned the boy's name, neither one spoke about him running away, neither one spoke about the wound.

y12.text: But Siddhartha knew what his friend was thinking. He thought, the boy would have thrown away or broken the oar in order to get even and in order to keep them from following him. And in fact, there was no oar left in the boat. Vasudeva pointed to the bottom of the boat and looked at his friend with a smile, as if he wanted to say: "Don't you see what your son is trying to tell you? Don't you see that he doesn't want to be followed?" But he did not say this in words. He started making a new oar. But Siddhartha bid his farewell, to look for the runaway. Vasudeva did not stop him.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha patiently tries to win over his grieving, spoiled son.
Siddhartha sends the boy back to the city at once.
Siddhartha forces his son to work in the field to forget the city.
Siddhartha mostly ignores the boy.
A.explanation: He "did not force him," did chores for him, and "hoped to win him over, by friendly patience." Forcing work reverses this. He does not send the boy away here. He picks "the best piece of the meal for him," so he does not ignore him.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what was missing from the boat?
options: Vasudeva's axe
The ropes and the coins
The oar
The sail
A.explanation: The passage says "there was no oar left in the boat." The basket of coins was taken earlier, and ropes are not mentioned here. The boat has no sail. Vasudeva carried the axe himself. The missing oar shows that the boy has taken the boat and gone.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "pampered" most nearly means
options: neglected
brave
sick
spoiled
A.explanation: The boy "had grown up in the habits of rich people, accustomed to finer food, to a soft bed," so pampered means spoiled. "Neglected" is the opposite. "Brave" and "sick" do not fit a child used to comfort and servants.

A.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha's love for the boy is
options: something he keeps hidden
a passing feeling soon forgotten
weaker than his wish to follow Vasudeva's advice
stronger than what he knows to be wise
A.explanation: "Stronger than the knowledge was his love for the boy," so love outweighs wisdom. He simply cannot follow his friend's advice, so following Vasudeva's advice is wrong. He loves "thus blindly," not briefly. He does not hide it from Vasudeva.

A.prompt: What does Vasudeva believe about the boy?
options: He is not in a place where he can thrive.
He will soon love the hut and want to stay forever.
He is simply lazy and needs work.
He should be beaten into obeying.
A.explanation: Vasudeva says "your son is not in the place where he can prosper." He expects no new love for the hut. He calls the boy "that young bird... accustomed to a different life," not lazy. He later approves that the boy is not beaten, not urging beating.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "I'm seeing that you are tormenting yourself, I'm seeing that you're in grief."
"Your son, my dear, is worrying you, and he is also worrying me."
"your son is not in the place where he can prosper."
"I asked the river, O friend, many times I have asked it."
A.explanation: Only "your son is not in the place where he can prosper" states his belief about the boy. "I asked the river" says how he sought an answer. "You are tormenting yourself" concerns Siddhartha. "Is worrying you" shows concern but not his belief about where the boy belongs.

A.prompt: The phrases "every naughtiness with a smile, every insult with friendliness" mainly serve to
options: list the boy's daily chores
show how the father's kindness only frustrates the boy
praise the boy's good nature
describe the boy's polite manners toward the old men
A.explanation: The father answers everything with kindness, and "this very thing was the hated trick of this old sneak," so his kindness frustrates the boy. The boy is not polite. These are not chores. The phrases describe the father, not praise for the boy.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha gives up and turns back home at once.
Siddhartha fears robbers on the dark forest road.
Though he sees the search is useless, Siddhartha runs on to see his son once more.
Siddhartha finds his son lost in the forest and carries him back.
A.explanation: He realizes "his search was useless," yet "he ran without stopping... just to perhaps see him one more time." He does not find the boy. He does not turn back. He knows the boy is not "in any danger," so no fear of robbers.

A.prompt: According to Vasudeva, why will they build a raft?
options: To get their boat back
To go fishing downriver
To chase the boy into the city
To cross to Kamala's garden
A.explanation: Vasudeva says, "We will build a raft... to get our boat back." He says "him, you shall let run along," so following by force is wrong. Fishing is not mentioned. Kamala's garden is not the purpose. Their plan is simply to recover the boat the boy has taken.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "cling" most nearly means
options: push away
hold on to
call loudly
teach
A.explanation: He "was not allowed to cling him," meaning to hold on to his son. "Push away" is the opposite. "Call loudly" and "teach" do not fit the sense of holding on. The word describes how the father holds on to his son though he should let him go.

A.prompt: The silence between the two men suggests that
options: Vasudeva silently blames Siddhartha
they understand each other without words
they are angry and refuse to speak
they are lost
A.explanation: "Neither one talked about what had happened," yet Siddhartha smiles at Vasudeva's face and shares the bananas, showing understanding without words. No anger is shown. No blame is expressed. They walk "home to the ferry," so they are not lost.

A.prompt: The comparison of his love to "a wound" suggests that it
options: was caused by the boy's fists
has healed completely, leaving no trace of grief behind
is a battle injury
causes him real pain
A.explanation: He felt love "in his heart, like a wound," a wound into which a knife might be turned, so it hurts. It has not healed; it still "had to become a blossom." No battle is meant. The wound is a comparison, not a real injury from the boy.

B.prompt: According to Vasudeva, what is stronger than force?
options: Teachings
Love
Riches
Anger
B.explanation: Vasudeva lists "'soft' is stronger than 'hard,' water stronger than rocks, love stronger than force." Riches are not in his list. Teachings and anger are not named as stronger than force. Vasudeva believes that patient love is stronger than force or command.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "devout" most nearly means
options: lazy
religious
rich
angry
B.explanation: The father is "perhaps a very devout man, perhaps a saint," so devout means religious. "Rich" describes the boy's old life, not his father. "Angry" and "lazy" do not fit a "good, kind, soft man." The word describes the pious, religious habits of the two old men, which the boy scorns.

B.prompt: Vasudeva's words suggest that the boy is
options: doing what Siddhartha himself failed to do
in great danger and must be found by nightfall
sorry for leaving
too young to travel alone
B.explanation: He says "He's doing what you've failed to do yourself. He's taking care of himself." He says the boy "knows how to get around," so no great danger. "He is no child any more." Nothing suggests he is sorry. By running away, the boy repeats what Siddhartha once did to his own father.

B.prompt: What does the passage say Siddhartha has become since his son arrived?
options: A rich man again
A Samana again
A great teacher visited for advice
A childlike person, lost to love
B.explanation: "Now he, Siddhartha, had also become completely a childlike person... lost to a love." He has not become a teacher or rich man. He is not a Samana again; he is loving another person foolishly. Through his love for his son, Siddhartha has become like the childlike people he once pitied.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "was nevertheless renewed in one respect, enriched by one thing."
"and was nevertheless in bliss"
"now he, Siddhartha, had also become completely a childlike person"
"this strongest and strangest of all passions"
B.explanation: Only "had also become completely a childlike person" names what he has become. "This strongest and strangest of all passions" names the feeling, not the change in him. "Nevertheless in bliss" and "enriched by one thing" describe effects of the love.

B.prompt: The series of questions beginning "Don't you shackle him with your love?" mainly serves to
options: praise Siddhartha's strictness
ask Siddhartha for advice about Vasudeva's own children
change the subject
argue that even kindness can force the boy
B.explanation: The questions show kindness can "shackle" and "force" the boy, building Vasudeva's argument. Vasudeva has no children mentioned. He questions, not praises, Siddhartha's method, and Siddhartha is not strict. The questions stay on the subject of the boy. The questions show that even gentle love can become a chain for the boy.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha knows what is wise but cannot act against his love.
Siddhartha falls asleep quickly that night.
Siddhartha learns something wholly new from Vasudeva and follows his advice.
Siddhartha stops loving the boy.
B.explanation: "Vasudeva had told him nothing, he had not already thought and known," but "stronger than the knowledge was his love." He did not learn anything new or follow the advice. He "could not sleep for a long time." He loves the boy blindly.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "pursuer" most nearly means
options: one who follows after
a robber
a guide
one who hides from others
B.explanation: The boy would "conceal himself from him, the pursuer," so the pursuer is the one following. Hiding is what the boy does. A robber and a guide do not fit Siddhartha chasing his son. The word describes Siddhartha as he follows the runaway boy toward the city.

B.prompt: The words Vasudeva seems to say in quotation marks mainly serve to
options: show Siddhartha's growing anger
show what he means without his saying it aloud
show the boy's message
report a long speech that Vasudeva gives aloud
B.explanation: The narrator gives "as if he wanted to say" and then "he did not say this in words," showing unspoken meaning. No speech is given. The quoted lines are Vasudeva's, about the boy. Siddhartha is not shown angry. The quoted words show what Vasudeva means, though he says nothing aloud.

options: wishes the boy had never come to him
fears the boy's anger and his words
respects the boy's grief and hopes love will win him
plans to punish the boy until he learns to obey
B.explanation: He "honoured his mourning" and "hoped to win him over, by friendly patience." He "did not force him," so no punishment. Nothing shows regret at the boy's coming. He is not afraid of the boy. He waits patiently, hoping his love will slowly win over the angry boy.

B.prompt: The passage is presented mainly from the point of view of
options: Kamala
the monks
Vasudeva, who watches with concern
the boy
B.explanation: The passage tells what the boy feels: "He was bored by this father," the father's kindness was "the hated trick of this old sneak." Vasudeva is not the viewpoint here. Kamala has died. No monks appear. The passage shows events mainly through the boy's angry and scornful eyes.

B.prompt: How does Passage 2 support the advice in Passage 1?
options: It tells the story of Vasudeva's wife.
It argues that a patient father's love can spare a son all suffering.
It argues that no one can be spared his own path, even by love.
It changes the subject to the river.
B.explanation: Passage 1 says the boy belongs elsewhere; Passage 2 says "you would not be able to take the slightest part of his destiny upon yourself." That denies love can protect him. Vasudeva's wife is not mentioned. Passage 2 stays on the son.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: No one can take another person's destiny upon himself.
The boy will die alone in the forest.
Vasudeva has no son of his own.
A loving father can always keep his son from his own mistakes.
C.explanation: "Even if you would die ten times for him, you would not be able to take the slightest part of his destiny." The second choice reverses the point. The boy's death is not predicted. Vasudeva's children are not discussed. Vasudeva argues that every person must find his own path and suffer his own fate.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha's earlier sense of being set apart from the childlike people
options: came from his long travels and trade
came partly from never having loved another so fully
was mistaken about their wealth
proved that he was wiser than them in every single way
C.explanation: He had never given himself completely to another person, and that seemed to set him apart from the childlike. Now love makes him like them. The passage does not call him wiser in every way. Wealth and travels are not the reason.

C.prompt: The phrases "thus blindly, thus sufferingly, thus unsuccessfully, and yet thus happily" mainly serve to
options: show that he has stopped loving the boy
list the boy's faults one by one, from worst to least
build up his love's pain and end on a paradox
describe Vasudeva's patience
C.explanation: Three painful words pile up, then "and yet thus happily" adds a contradiction, a paradox. They describe his love, not the boy's faults. They show he still loves. Vasudeva is not described here. The series builds his blind, painful love and ends with the surprising word "happily."

C.prompt: What does Siddhartha realize at the garden gate?
options: His son is hiding among the monks in the garden.
Kamala is still alive somewhere.
His desire was foolish, and he cannot help his son.
He should become a monk himself.
C.explanation: He realized "that his desire was foolish... that he could not help his son." The boy is not found in the garden. Kamala is dead. He sees monks but does not decide to join them. At the gate he realises his son must go his own way, without his help.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "After having been standing by the gate of the garden for a long time"
"that he could not help his son, that he was not allowed to cling him."
"Deeply, he felt the love for the runaway in his heart, like a wound"
"that it had to become a blossom and had to shine."
C.explanation: Only "he could not help his son" states his realization. "Felt the love... like a wound" describes the feeling. "Standing by the gate" sets the scene. "It had to become a blossom" describes what the wound must become, not what he realized about his son.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "inferior" most nearly means
options: hungry
older
stronger
lesser
C.explanation: "Don't you make him feel inferior every day" means lesser or lower. "Stronger" is the opposite. "Older" and "hungry" do not fit how kindness makes him feel. The word describes how the boy feels beside the two old men he despises.

C.prompt: Calling the boy "That young bird is accustomed to a different life, to a different nest" suggests that he
options: belongs in a different kind of home
is very small and weak
sings well
will soon fly off to live in the forest
C.explanation: A young bird used to "a different nest" belongs to another home; Vasudeva means the city. The bird is a comparison, so living with birds is wrong. Size and singing are not the point of the comparison. The bird image shows that the boy was raised for a rich house, not a hut.

C.prompt: Vasudeva's choice not to stop Siddhartha suggests that he
options: is too weak to argue
wants Siddhartha to bring the boy back by force
lets his friend learn for himself
does not care
C.explanation: "Vasudeva did not stop him," though he knows the search is useless, letting him learn. He has advised against force. Nothing shows weakness. He makes a new oar and cares, as the smile shows. Vasudeva understands that Siddhartha must learn this lesson through his own experience, as Siddhartha once did when he left home.

C.prompt: The sentence beginning "Nevertheless, he ran without stopping" mainly serves to
options: show that he has found the boy's footprints
show his fear for the boy's safety
end the search
show his desire overriding what he knows
C.explanation: He knows the boy is safe and the search useless; "Nevertheless" shows desire overriding reason. No footprints are found. He was "not worried," so not fear. He runs on, so the search continues. He runs on although he knows the search is useless, driven by his love.

C.prompt: The repeated phrase "neither one" mainly serves to
options: stress how much is left unsaid between the friends
list the people they met that day
show that the two men have quarrelled and stopped talking
describe the ferry
C.explanation: "Neither one talked... neither one mentioned... neither one spoke" stresses silence. They share bananas and smile, so no quarrel. No people are listed. The ferry is only where they return. The repetition shows how much the two friends understand without saying it.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 complicate the love described in Passage 1?
options: It shows Siddhartha punishing the boy.
It shows the boy returning his father's love with equal tenderness.
It shows Vasudeva taking the boy away.
It shows the boy finding that love tiresome and hateful.
C.explanation: Passage 1 shows blind love; in Passage 2 the boy "was bored by this father," calling his kindness "the hated trick." He does not return the love. Vasudeva does not take him. Siddhartha answers insults "with friendliness," not punishment. Passage 2 shows that the boy feels his father's patient love as a burden.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 change Siddhartha's state in Passage 1?
options: He finds the boy at the gate and they return home together happily.
His urgent desire gives way to the knowledge that it was foolish.
He grows angry with Vasudeva.
He decides to live in the city.
C.explanation: In Passage 1 he runs "just to satisfy his desire"; in Passage 2 he "realised that his desire was foolish." He does not find the boy. Vasudeva is not blamed. He sits by the road, with no plan to live in the city.
